t: LeetCode 1818 - Minimum Absolute Sum Difference: One Swap, Binary Search the Best
o: The absolute sum difference is simply the total L1 mismatch between two aligned arrays. You may copy any single value from nums1 over any single position of nums1 (at most one replacement), trying to shrink this total as much as possible. Only positions with positive current difference can improve, and replacing position i with value v changes the total by |nums1[i]-nums2[i]| - |v-nums2[i]|; since just one move is allowed, we want the single largest such saving. In example 3 the original total is 27 and copying 10 over the leading 1 turns |1-9|=8 into |10-9|=1, saving 7 for the answer 20. With n up to 10^5, checking every candidate value for every position (n^2 work) is too slow, so the replacement pool should be kept sorted and searched.
k: One allowed replacement means maximizing a single saving: cur_i minus the distance from nums2[i] to its nearest element of nums1.
The pool of replacements is nums1 itself - sort a copy once and binary-search the value closest to each nums2[i].
Accumulate totals in 64-bit and apply the modulus once at the very end.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Over All Replacements
a.i: Compute the base total, then for every position try every candidate value from nums1, tracking the biggest improvement. This nails the semantics (including that skipping the replacement is allowed when no saving exists) but does O(n^2) work - fine to propose first, too slow to submit for n = 10^5.
s: Sum cur_i = |nums1[i] - nums2[i]| over all i
For each i and each candidate v in nums1 compute the saving cur_i - |v - nums2[i]|
a.t: O(n^2) - every position scans the whole replacement pool; will TLE at n = 10^5, shown to build intuition.

a.n: Approach 2: Sort Once, Binary Search Each Target
a.i: Sort a copy of nums1. For each position, the optimal replacement is whichever neighbor sits immediately around nums2[i] in sorted order, found by binary search (lower_bound); checking both the insertion point and the element before it covers the nearest value on either side. The best per-position saving across all positions is subtracted from the precomputed total.
s: Sort a copy of nums1 and compute the initial total
For each i, binary search for nums2[i] in sorted1
Take the closer of sorted1[j] and sorted1[j-1]; record saving cur_i - |closest - nums2[i]|

c.python:
from bisect import bisect_left

class Solution:
    def minAbsoluteSumDiff(self, nums1: List[int], nums2: List[int]) -> int:
        MOD = 10**9 + 7
        sorted1 = sorted(nums1)
        n = len(nums1)
        total = 0
        best = 0
        for i in range(n):
            cur = abs(nums1[i] - nums2[i])
            total += cur
            j = bisect_left(sorted1, nums2[i])
            if j < n:
                best = max(best, cur - abs(sorted1[j] - nums2[i]))
            if j > 0:
                best = max(best, cur - abs(sorted1[j - 1] - nums2[i]))
        return (total - best) % MOD

a.t: O(n log n) - one sort plus one binary search per position.
a.sp: O(n) - the sorted copy of nums1.

w: Jump straight to sort-plus-binary-search after stating the brute force in one sentence; that pairing is what the interviewer wants to hear. Pitfalls: forgetting the second candidate left of the insertion point, applying mod to intermediate negative numbers (subtract before taking the modulus), and misreading that the replacement must reuse a value already in nums1. Follow-ups: allow k replacements - greedily take the k largest savings with a heap; support a dynamic nums1 with an ordered multiset for O(log n) queries.
